content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued updated recommendations on the use of antenatal corticosteroids to improve outcomes for preterm births. These guidelines are based on the latest evidence and aim to enhance the quality of care for pregnant women at risk of preterm delivery and their newborns. The recommendations supersede those published in 2015 and are intended for healthcare professionals, policymakers, and program managers involved in maternal and neonatal care. Preterm birth complications are the leading cause of neonatal deaths and deaths in children under five years of age. Babies born preterm are at higher risk of severe illnesses during childhood, including respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular hemorrhage, necrotizing enterocolitis, and sepsis, as well as long-term conditions like chronic lung disease and neurological disabilities. Interventions provided to mothers before or during pregnancy, and to preterm newborns after birth, can significantly reduce mortality and morbidity associated with preterm birth. Antenatal corticosteroids, such as intramuscular dexamethasone or betamethasone (administered in a total dose of 24 mg in divided doses), are recommended for women at high risk of imminent preterm birth. These corticosteroids cross the placenta and promote the structural maturity of fetal lungs, including surfactant production, which improves lung compliance and reduces respiratory-related complications in preterm newborns. The updated recommendations were developed using a systematic process that included identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, and assessing the quality of evidence using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology. The Guideline Development Group (GDG), composed of international experts and stakeholders, formulated the recommendations based on evidence-to-decision criteria, including intervention effects, values, resource use, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The recommendations include one overarching recommendation and nine sub-recommendations, which address specific contexts such as gestational age, interval between therapy and birth, multiple births, preterm premature rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, elective cesarean sections in the late preterm period, hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, fetal growth restriction, and diabetes in pregnancy. The GDG also provided guidance on the choice of corticosteroids and the use of repeat courses of corticosteroids for women who remain at risk of preterm birth after completing an initial course. The primary audience for these recommendations includes healthcare professionals responsible for developing national and local health guidelines, as well as those directly providing care to pregnant women and preterm infants, such as obstetricians, pediatricians, midwives, and nurses. The guidelines are also relevant for policymakers, program managers, and organizations involved in maternal and neonatal health. The WHO emphasizes that these recommendations are women-centered and aim to improve maternal and neonatal health outcomes globally. The organization encourages the development of job aids and training tools to support healthcare workers in implementing these guidelines effectively.
